questions.q: List the five supporting characters in "We're Not Afraid to Die" and state one specific action each takes during the crisis (January 2–6).
questions.a: Mary: takes the wheel for crucial hours while the captain repairs the hull; Jonathan (6): asks "Are we going to die?" then says "we aren't afraid of dying if we can all be together"; Suzanne (7): hides her severe head injury to avoid worrying her father, makes a morale-boosting card; Larry Vigil: pumps continuously for 36+ hours, steers course 185°; Herb Seigler: pumps "like a madman" alongside Larry, remains cheerful and optimistic. A wrong answer (e.g., vague roles like "they helped") reveals the student cannot distinguish individual agency and textual evidence, treating supporting characters as an undifferentiated group.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how Mary's reaction to the disaster differs from the captain's reaction in the first 24 hours after the wave strike.
questions.a: The captain focuses on technical survival tasks (repairing holes, pumping, navigation calculations) and suppresses emotion to maintain command. Mary immediately alerts him to the flooding ("We're sinking!"), then takes the wheel without being asked and holds it for "all those crucial hours," providing steady steering while he works below. She also finds food (corned beef, crackers) for the first meal in two days. A wrong answer that says "both were scared" or "both worked hard" misses the gendered division of labor the text portrays: the captain as problem-solver, Mary as sustainer of both vessel and family morale.

questions.q: Based on Jonathan's dialogue on January 5 ("we aren't afraid of dying if we can all be together"), predict how he would react if the captain had been swept overboard permanently. Justify using his established character traits.
questions.a: Jonathan would likely suppress his grief to support Suzanne and Mary, mirroring Suzanne's hiding of her injury. Evidence: his matter-of-fact tone ("Why, you must be [the best captain]. You found the island") shows he processes fear through affirmation of others. He would probably take on a caretaker role for Sue, echoing the family's "togetherness" ethic. A wrong answer predicting hysteria or paralysis ignores the text's consistent portrayal of the children as emotionally resilient beyond their years.

questions.q: Compare the roles of the two crewmen (Larry and Herb) with the roles of the family members (Mary, Jonathan, Suzanne) in the survival effort. What does this comparison reveal about the author's view of professional skill vs. emotional bonds?
questions.a: Larry and Herb provide technical labor: pumping, steering, maintaining equipment — their professionalism keeps the boat afloat physically. The family provides emotional architecture: Mary's steering endurance, Sue's silent courage, Jon's philosophical anchor ("we aren't afraid..."). The text values both but suggests emotional bonds are the ultimate survival mechanism: the captain's navigation succeeds only because the children's morale card renews his determination. A wrong answer listing only physical tasks misses the thematic argument that "togetherness" (emotional) enables technical competence to bear fruit.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Suzanne is the most courageous character in the story." Defend or refute using at least three pieces of textual evidence.
questions.a: Defensible. Evidence 1: She suffers a "big bump," two black eyes, a deep arm cut, and a recurring blood clot requiring six operations, yet says "I didn't want to worry you when you were trying to save us all." Evidence 2: She moves "painfully" to the chartroom to deliver a handmade morale card. Evidence 3: Her card's message — "Oh, how I love you both... let's hope for the best" — actively sustains the captain's will. Refutation would require arguing another character shows greater courage (e.g., captain's physical struggle), but Sue's silent endurance while injured is uniquely highlighted by the narrator's closing reflection. A wrong answer choosing the captain ignores the narrator's explicit final focus on Sue's sacrifice.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from Herb Seigler's perspective on the night of January 3, capturing his professional assessment of the ship's condition and his private thoughts about the family.
questions.a: "Jan 3, 0200 hrs. Pumps holding. Rib frames smashed to keel — she won't make Australia. Larry and I can keep her afloat another day, maybe two. The skipper's running on fumes, but those kids... the girl's half-blind, the boy talks like a philosopher. The wife steers like she was born to it. We're not just crew anymore. We're family." A poor answer would focus only on mechanical details or generic fear, missing Herb's textual characterization as "cheerful and optimistic under the direst stress" who observes the family dynamic professionally yet personally.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of supporting characters involves examining the traits, actions, dialogue, and ______ of secondary figures in a narrative to understand how they advance the plot, develop themes, and reveal aspects of the protagonist through contrast and interaction.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are on a ______ ship in the middle of the Indian Ocean with your family and two hired crewmen.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can write a structured character sketch for each supporting character (Mary, Jonathan, Suzanne, Larry, Herb) using the PEEL method (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link), citing specific textual evidence to explain their contribution to the themes of survival, family unity, and resilience.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ you are on a sinking ship in the middle of the Indian Ocean with your family and two hired crewmen.
